title: Timebox your way to product market fit: limit tries per hypothesis
summary: Garry Tan argues founders fail by not trying enough distinct hypotheses, so they should explicitly timebox each product-market hypothesis (a set of people plus a problem) and move on. He breaks failure into acquisition problems and not-a-real-problem, and lists levers for retention and pilot expansion.

principles.text: You have a finite number of tries; timebox each one so you can try more things and maximize your odds of success.
principles.quote: you have a finite number of tries. But if you timebox your tries, you'll get to try a lot more things. And that will maximize your chance of success.

principles.text: A product-market hypothesis is a specific set of reachable people plus a problem to solve for them.
principles.quote: A set of **people** that you can reach, and

principles.text: Diagnose failure in order: first can you get people to know and use it, then is it a real problem.
principles.quote: A, it's a real problem, but you **can't get people to know about it and use it**, or, B, it's **not a real problem**. In that order!

principles.text: For acquisition, try many channels instead of repeating one or two; there are no silver bullets, only lead ones.
principles.quote: The most common failure point when working on customer acquisition is getting stuck on one or two things, and trying those, over and over and over again, doing more of what doesn't work.

principles.text: Pilots that don't expand signal a product that doesn't stick; you need expansion and net retention to raise a Series A.
principles.quote: You need expansion. You need net retention. And if you can't, this isn't something people want.

principles.text: Set the timebox so it is neither too short nor too long: too short abandons something that could work, too long burns runway.
principles.quote: **Too short,** and you may have given up on something that could have worked. **Too long,** and you've wasted your time. You'll never get that time back.
